A New England shortline that you can model, Pt.II:

The Claremont & Concord Rwy.

With its little red GE diesels, the C&C was a classic Pinsly operation/Scott Whitney

SCOTT WHITNEY: CLAREMONT, NH; NOV., 1980

The C&C's 44-tonner No. 31 has just crossed the Sugar River and
is turning from Main onto Union St. Behind the engine is the for-

Maine of the late steam era your

mind immediately conjures up im-
ages of ancient Moguls trundling down
a cinder ballasted right of way and
rolling through wooden covered
bridges. And so it was with the Clare-
mont branch of the B&M right up until
the mid 1950’s. The Claremont branch
was certainly neither the last B&M
line to host steam nor was it the first
B&M line to be sold off as a shortline,
however, it was the best known of them
all. Much has already been written
about the line including an excellent
book by Edgar T. Mead titled Through
Covered Bridges To Concord (ong out
of print).

O) “OL UMBIA
RAILWAY

During the mid part of the century,
the Boston & Maine decided that the
Claremont branch was not a going con-
cern and seriously worked toward the
idea of giving up the operation. It was
also about this time that shortline en-
trepreneur Samuel Pinsly was starting
his large collection of shortlines. Mr.
Pinsly would eventually go on to own
and operate six different former B&M
or B&M owned operations; the Clare-
mont Branch was among these.

Pinsly had already bought the little
Claremont Railway and actively pur-
sued the B&M’s Claremont branch
which would allow the two to be com-
bined into one efficient operation. On
December 17, 1954, the Claremont &

mer Presto Grain Co., which has since been converted into hous-
ing for the elderly. To the right is the spur that served River St.

Concord Railway became official. In-
cluded in the deal were the buildings,
land and some equipment, which in-
cluded one locomotive and a gas elec-
tric passenger set.

Unfortunately, it was to be a shotgun
wedding for the poor Claremont Rail-
way. Within an incredibly short time
period the wire came down from over
the little electric road and most all of
the equipment was dissected for the
various metals and scrapped. It was
decided to utilize the former B&M en-
ginehouse at Claremont Junction
rather than the Claremont Railway’s
carbarn for locomotive storage and re-
pair. Soon enough the operation settled
into a regular routine.

DECEMBER 1993
